answer: I would like to talk about a man my whole family looks up to. The older person I respect most is my grandfather, who is now in his eighties but still remarkably sharp. He lives with my grandmother in our ancestral village home not far from Sirajganj, and we visit them as often as we can. He worked the family land for most of his life, and he lived through some genuinely difficult times, and yet he has never become bitter or cynical about life. In terms of what he is like, he is gentle and quick-witted, and he still wakes up at dawn to walk around the fields. He is also incredibly [[humble]] about his own achievements, rarely talking about the hardships he overcame. I love listening to his stories, because each one seems to carry a subtle lesson without ever being preachy. Despite his age, he remains genuinely [[open-minded]], curious about new technology and interested in what young people think. He even asks me to show him cricket highlights on my phone, and he has strong opinions about every player. What I respect most is his [[wisdom]]; whenever the family faces a problem, he has this quiet way of putting things in perspective. I also think there is something we can all learn from his [[contentment]]; he seems at peace with his life in a way that is rare. Honestly, I hope I can grow old with even half of his grace and good humour.

followUps.q: Do you spend a lot of time with him?
followUps.answer: Not as much as I would like, because of work. But whenever we visit the village, I make sure to sit with him for a while, usually in the courtyard with tea, just listening to him [[reminisce]].

followUps.q: Do you think older people are respected enough in your country?
followUps.answer: Mostly, yes. Respect for elders is deeply rooted in Bangladeshi culture, and grandparents often live with their families. However, I think that tradition is weakening slightly in the big cities.
